title.en: Kagssagssuk, the Homeless Boy Who Became a Strong Man
title.zh: 流浪孤兒卡格薩克舒克

region.en: Smith Sound, Polar Eskimo country, Northwest Greenland
region.zh: 西北格陵蘭史密斯海峽極地因紐特之地

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition (Polar Eskimo, Smith Sound); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'Kagssagssuk, the homeless boy who became a strong man', eBook #28932

summary.en: The Great Fire, whip of live ribbon seal, frizzles a whole house of noisy children — only homeless Kagssagssuk survives on the drying frame, and the village punishes him for the truth. Ground down by Umerdlugtoq, who hauls him by the nostrils, and by a beating grandmother, he trains by stone-twirling with a pitying giant until stones sing 'leu-leu-leu' in the air, then hauls an umiak from the ice, kills three bears with his fists, casts the wicked grandmother on her own fire, and holds Umerdlugtoq out over a precipice by the nostrils — 'Do not fear; for you never used to kill me.' Later his pride turns him to crushing children, and his fellows harpoon him.
summary.zh: 『大火』以活環斑海豹為鞭，將喧嘩的孩童們燒成焦炭——流浪兒卡格薩克舒克因藏於晾架而倖存，村民卻罵他撒謊。他受大人物烏默德盧格托克提鼻羞辱、惡祖母毒打；與悲憫的巨人推石練力，石在空中『嚕嚕』作響；拖出冰封大舟、赤手殺三熊、將惡祖母擲入火中，再把烏默德盧格托克提鼻懸於懸崖——『別怕；你從前從未殺過我。』後來他得勢驕橫，竟捏碎孩童，終被同伴魚叉所殺。

sensitivity.note: Polar Eskimo tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. The killing of the wicked grandmother and of children in the coda is presented as told in the source.

passages.text: When the men and women had gone to a spirit calling, the children left behind played in one big house, and homeless Kagssagssuk, alone outside, warned them: 'You must not make so much noise, or the Great Fire will come.' They would not believe him — and the Great Fire appeared: he had a great live ribbon seal for a whip, with long claws, and he began dragging the children out through the passage, each one frizzled up as it was drawn. Little Kagssagssuk had cried to be lifted to the drying frame under the roof for his gloves, and so escaped; the Great Fire, going away, touched a hanging skin with his finger. None of the gathered villagers believed the boy — 'You have killed them yourself' — so he dared them to make a noise like the children did, and the Great Fire came again; but this time the people poured boiling oil over its living whip, and it went away. From that time the village was unkind to the boy who had told the truth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Kagssagssuk, the homeless boy who became a strong man'; not verbatim.

passages.text: He had lived in the house of Umerdlugtoq, a great man, but now he was forced to stay outside; if he stepped in only to dry his boots, Umerdlugtoq lifted him up by the nostrils and cast him over the high threshold. One grandmother beat him whenever she could; the other, his mother's mother, took pity and dried his clothes. They fed him on tough walrus hide, and he gnawed it with the help of a little stone he kept in his breeches; he slept among the dogs and warmed himself on the roof in the warm air of the smoke hole, to be hauled down by the nostrils again. Wandering one spring day, he met a giant cutting up his catch; his cry for meat was too small to hear until the giant said 'Bring me luck' and threw down a little piece, thinking it one of the dead who asked. Kagssagssuk, already having helping spirits, made the piece a big one and ate his fill.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Kagssagssuk, the homeless boy who became a strong man'; not verbatim.

passages.text: When his hidden meat turned out stolen by the giant himself, the giant, feeling kindly, proposed they play together: pushing stones until they twirled. At first Kagssagssuk fell backwards; then he ceased falling and could move the stones, each larger than the last, until he could make even the biggest twirl in the air, the stone saying 'leu-leu-leu-leu' as it flew. Seeing them equal in strength, the giant said: 'Now you have become a strong man. But since it was by my fault that you lost that piece of meat, I will by magic means cause three bears to come right down to your village.' Kagssagssuk went home, hauled an umiak free of the ice in the night to show his strength, and was mocked for it by Umerdlugtoq.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Kagssagssuk, the homeless boy who became a strong man'; not verbatim.

passages.text: When three bears appeared exactly as the giant had said, Kagssagssuk borrowed his grandmother's boots and went out, treading so hard the footprints seemed made in soft snow. He grasped the biggest bear — a mother with two half-grown cubs — with his naked fists and wrung its neck; then hammered the cubs' skulls together. Carrying the bear over his shoulders and a cub under each arm as if they were no more than hares, he skinned them and cooked the meat on a big flat stone for his kind grandmother — and cast the wicked grandmother on the fire, where all burned up but her stomach. Umerdlugtoq fled with his wives to a tent on a precipice edge; up came Kagssagssuk, caught him by the nostrils and held him out over the edge, shaking him until they burst: 'Do not fear; I am not going to kill you. For you never used to kill me.' Then he called out from inside the tent, 'I am in here with your wives!' — took vengeance on all who had ill-treated him, went south, and lived there. But being so strong he grew filled with the desire to be feared and began catching hold of children and crushing them; therefore his fellow-villagers harpooned him one day when he was out in his kayak.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Kagssagssuk, the homeless boy who became a strong man'; not verbatim.

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition (West Greenland); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'Qasiagssaq, the great liar', eBook #28932

summary.en: Sleepless, seal-less Qasiagssaq resolves to live by lies: he steals a fellow-hunter's black seal and shows off its narwhal-tusk tow-line; hammers his own knee-caps and kayaks to pieces and piles iceberg fragments on himself to fake an iceberg calving; ties his bladder floats to a stone to counterfeit a struck walrus; whistles at a speckled seal rather than pierce its skin with harpoon holes, losing it; fakes a dead daughter's name to beg beads, a cooking pot, and loads of food; and lures his starving in-laws with tales of seals daily thrown away. At last he announces a dead whale that is never there, ness after ness, and the exasperated villagers kill him.
summary.zh: 失眠無獵的瓜西亞克舒克決定靠謊言過活：竊取同伴的黑海豹、炫耀獨角鯨牙拖繩；自錘膝蓋、砸爛皮艇、懷揣冰塊，偽稱冰山崩塌；將浮囊繫石假冒中鯨海象；為保全妻子褲料皮而對海豹吹哨，反使其逃逸；假冒亡女之名騙取珠串、炊鍋與食糧；又以『村中海豹日日棄置』誘饑餓的岳母來投。最後他謊稱發現鯨屍，引眾船一岬又一岬地空跑，眾人終於將他殺死。

sensitivity.note: West Greenland tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. The name-stealingmourning episode is a documented but sensitive social custom; presented as told.

passages.text: Qasiagssaq was a great liar who could never sleep well at night and always woke his fellow-villagers for the morning hunt — but never brought home anything himself. 'It is no use my trying to be a hunter; I may as well make up some lie or other,' he said, and that very day, seeing a fellow-villager towing a big black seal to an island to land it, he rowed round behind the man, stole it, and towed it home. His wife shaded her eyes and watched his kayak come in with its catch; the villagers cried 'Here is Qasiagssaq has made a catch' and admired the deep black markings and the tow-line thick with trappings of the finest narwhal tusk — 'I have had it a long time,' he said. The last kayak in told the truth: he had landed that seal on the island and found it gone. That evening a voice asked at the window for the tow-line back, and Qasiagssaq sprang up with it — while his wife said, as she would say again and again, 'When Qasiagssaq does such things, one cannot but feel shame for him.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Qasiagssaq, the great liar'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Rowing home empty-handed another day, he laid one knee across a stone and hammered both knee-caps to pieces with another stone, then battered his kayak's woodwork to bits, piled fragments of iceberg upon it and even inside his raven-skin clothes, and rowed home: 'An iceberg calved.' Two women had watched the whole performance from the shore and told it all; his wife only said her usual 'shame,' and he frightened her with 'Hrrrr!' Later he laid a long stone on his kayak, rowed out among waiting kayakers, tied his two small bladder floats to the stone, and rowed away as fast as he could — announcing on coming in that he had struck a great walrus which had gone down with his floats. But the kayaker still out brought back the floats themselves: 'They had been tied to a stone, and the knot had worked loose.' 'When Qasiagssaq does such things, one cannot but feel shame for him.' 'Hrrrr!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Qasiagssaq, the great liar'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Once, coming on a speckled seal crawled up on the ice, he lifted his harpoon to throw — then looked at the point and laid it down again: 'Would it not be a pity, now, for that skin, which is to be used to make breeches for my wife, to be pierced with holes by the point of a harpoon?' He began whistling to the seal, to take hold of it, and the seal went down; up again, whistled at again, down again — and did not come up any more. Hearing that an old couple in another village had lost their little daughter, he visited them and, clearing his throat, said loudly: 'To-day my little daughter Nipisartangivaq is doubtless crying at her mother's side as usual.' The mourners, grateful, gave him beads, a cooking pot, and great quantities of food for 'his little girl' — and more came with meat until the villagers said plainly: 'Qasiagssaq and his wife have no children.' The strangers would not even land: 'Then tell them to give us back the beads and the cooking pot.' 'Now you have lied again... one cannot but feel shame for you.' 'Hrrrr!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Qasiagssaq, the great liar'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Visiting his wife's mother, whose lamp was out of blubber and whose child cried for hunger, he lamented his own foolishness — 'Over in our village, seals are daily thrown away. You must come back with me to our place' — then hurried ahead and let her find nothing on his rubbish heap but carrion of ravens, one of which he 'caught in his snare' to cook on shoulder-blade lamp and pot. In time he came home crying: 'I have found a dead whale; to-morrow we must all go out in the umiak and cut it up.' Many umiaks and kayaks rowed east with him — 'Where is it?' 'Over there, beyond that little ness' — ness after ness, nothing to be seen. 'Qasiagssaq is lying as usual. Let us kill him.' 'Wait a little; let us first make sure that it is a lie, and if you do not see it, you may kill me' — and at last they did as they had said, and killed him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Qasiagssaq, the great liar'; not verbatim.
